title: Aspen Park Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Aspen Park wells have a 305-foot median depth. See local yields, water levels and modeled finished-well costs of $25,800-$42,500.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Aspen Park
intro_html:
In Aspen Park, finding water is a fractured-bedrock job. A nearby well can help you budget, but it cannot guarantee what your lot will produce. Local records show a median drilled depth of 305 feet and a median reported pump yield of 5.0 gpm.

These figures cover Colorado DWR permitted wells within 5 miles of Aspen Park, including the area toward Conifer. They describe the surrounding mountain well market, not just properties with an Aspen Park address. Depth, yield and water-level figures come from different subsets of those records.

sections.heading: A 305-Foot Budget Is a Starting Point in Aspen Park
sections.html:
Among the 7,785 wells reporting depth, the median is 305 feet and the middle half runs from 195 to 483 feet. That spread matters more to a drilling bid than the median alone: a contractor needs to explain how additional footage will be priced if productive fractures are deeper than expected. The 90th-percentile depth is 660 feet.

Permits overwhelmingly identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with Fractured Crystalline and Fractured Granite also listed. Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 0% of the records. In this granite and gneiss terrain, fracture location and connection drive results. A well near Conifer or farther toward Evergreen is context, not a depth promise for your parcel.

sections.heading: Aspen Park's Reported Yields Favor Modest Household Supply
sections.html:
The 3,925 wells with reported pump yields have a median of 5.0 gpm, with the middle half between 3.0 and 8.3 gpm. Most reported yields fall in the 5-15 gpm band, which accounts for 52%. Another 38% fall in the 1-5 gpm band.

For a buyer, the important caution is the 4% reporting under 1 gpm. A low-producing well may need storage and careful demand management; its suitability depends on recovery and household use, not just pump size. A permit-record yield is not a current performance guarantee. Ask for a sustained pumping and recovery test before relying on an existing well, especially if the seller reports seasonal shortages.

sections.heading: Water at 80 Feet Does Not Mean an 80-Foot Well
sections.html:
Only 421 records report static water level. Their median is 80 feet below ground, and the middle half spans 35-150 feet. Static level describes where water stands in a resting well, not the depth needed to intercept useful fractures. It should not be substituted for drilled depth when estimating cost.

Decade medians move from 40 feet in the 1960s to 135 feet in the 1990s, then become shallower: 120 feet in the 2000s and 100 feet in both the 2010s and 2020s. That is not a steady downward trend. These are measurements from different wells, not repeated monitoring of the same wells. They cannot establish a property-specific water-table decline.

sections.heading: An Established Well Area With Records Through 2025
sections.html:
The Aspen Park search area contains 11,280 permit records, with 7,605 recorded as constructed. Permit activity was greatest in the 1970s, with 3,186 permits, followed by 2,254 in the 1990s. The 2020s account for 286 permits, and the newest permit year is 2025. Issuance history is not the same as a count of operating wells.

The most active drillers listed are Living Water Systems Inc. (Goble, Robert), with 923 records; Aspen Drilling Company Inc (Beery, Leroy J.), with 873; and Walton, with 856. These are historical record totals, not confirmation of current availability. Domestic/household use accounts for 93% of permits, but the actual permit—not the neighborhood's typical use—controls what a buyer may do.

sections.heading: Budgeting a Finished Well in Aspen Park's Bedrock
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $65-$100 per foot for drilling fractured mountain bedrock. At the 305-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $19,800-$30,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $25,800-$42,500. These are planning figures, not a parcel-specific quote.

Get a written scope that distinguishes drilling from casing, grout, pump equipment and the connection to the house. Ask how deeper drilling, difficult rig access and unexpected ground conditions are handled. With the middle half of recorded depths reaching from 195 to 483 feet, treating the median-depth estimate as a fixed price leaves a buyer exposed to additional footage and equipment costs.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality Separately From Water Quantity
sections.html:
Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 29 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 45 historic mine features and 51 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. Those categories flag questions to investigate; they do not establish that an Aspen Park well is contaminated. A sampling location is not automatically a confirmed impact, and proximity alone does not prove a groundwater connection.

Have the water tested and use nearby site information to discuss appropriate additional testing with a qualified laboratory or environmental professional. Inspect the wellhead, casing and surface drainage as well. Fractured rock makes both yield and groundwater pathways uneven. Deeper drilling does not guarantee a productive well, so discuss unsuccessful drilling terms before work starts and keep septic placement part of the site review.

sections.heading: Before Buying an Aspen Park Lot, Fit the Whole Site
sections.html:
Start with nearby well records, then compare the parcel's terrain and access rather than assuming all mountain lots behave alike. Conifer is useful nearby context; Brook Forest and Indian Hills offer broader comparisons, but their wells should not replace records closest to the property. Review the DWR permit, construction report and any available pumping tests for an existing well.

For a new build, confirm allowable well use with DWR before budgeting outdoor watering or other demands. An exempt household-use permit is not blanket permission for irrigation. Coordinate the well location, septic system, house footprint, driveway and drilling-rig access before finalizing the site plan. On an existing home, make current yield and water-quality testing part of your purchase due diligence.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Aspen Park, Colorado?
faq.a: Wells reporting depth within 5 miles of Aspen Park have a median depth of 305 feet. The middle half runs from 195 to 483 feet, and the 90th percentile is 660 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make depths variable, so use nearby construction records to guide a bid rather than treating the median as a guaranteed stopping depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Aspen Park?
faq.a: The local model estimates $65-$100 per foot for fractured-bedrock drilling. At the 305-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $19,800-$30,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $25,800-$42,500. Get a site-specific bid that spells out access requirements, casing and grout, additional footage charges and equipment.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Aspen Park?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 5.0 gpm, with the middle half between 3.0 and 8.3 gpm. Of wells reporting yield, 4% are under 1 gpm. These records help screen a property, but a current pumping and recovery test is more useful for judging household supply and whether storage may be needed.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Aspen Park?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from permit records or location alone. The surrounding area has 29 mapped PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 45 historic mine features and 51 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those listings do not prove contamination in a particular well. Test the property's water and review nearby site details when selecting additional laboratory tests.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Aspen Park?
faq.a: The available records do not show a steady decline. Median static water depth was 135 feet in the 1990s, 120 feet in the 2000s and 100 feet in both the 2010s and 2020s. Only 421 records report static levels, and the decade groups contain different wells. They cannot establish a trend for an individual property.
